headline: Movies are an illusion—still images shown fast enough to trick your brain into seeing motion
universal_truth: Our perception can be fooled; reality and experience aren't always the same
fun_facts: Movies typically show 24 frames per second—24 still photographs every second
Your brain blends images shown faster than about 16 per second into smooth motion
The first audiences reportedly ran from the screen when they saw a train approaching
discussion_questions: Why does our brain combine still images into motion?
What other perception tricks do we experience daily?
How has the illusion of motion changed storytelling?

hook.script: Every movie you've ever watched is a lie. There is no motion on the screen—just still pictures, flashing by so fast your brain can't tell the difference. Twenty-four frozen moments per second, blurred into the illusion of life.

cliff.script: If movies are just still images, why do we see movement? Why doesn't our brain notice that each image is frozen? What creates the seamless illusion of motion?
cliff.prompt: Why do we see motion in still images?

options.text: Our brains blend images together when they change faster than we can process individually
options.response: Yes. This is called 'persistence of vision' and 'motion blur'—your brain fills gaps and blends frames into continuous movement.

options.text: The projector moves so fast that actual motion occurs between frames
options.response: There's no actual motion—the magic happens in your brain's interpretation...

fact1.title: Persistence of Vision
fact1.script: Your brain retains each image for a fraction of a second after it disappears. When images flash faster than this retention fades, they blend together. Your visual system literally can't keep up—and this creates the illusion of smooth motion.

fact2.title: 24 Frames
fact2.script: Movies settled on 24 frames per second as a balance: fast enough to appear smooth, slow enough to save film. This arbitrary number, chosen for practical reasons, became the standard we still use. Your brain adapts to whatever frame rate it's given.

fact3.title: First Audiences
fact3.script: When early audiences saw a train approaching on screen, some reportedly fled in panic. They couldn't distinguish the illusion from reality. Today we've learned to separate real from recorded—but our brains still respond emotionally as if it's real.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Our perception can be fooled. Movies prove that what we experience isn't always what's real—our brains construct reality from limited information. Question what seems obvious; appearances deceive.

outro.script: That's Day 122. Tomorrow, we'll explore how TV shows pictures. Until then, pause a video and see the frozen frame hiding inside the motion.

growTrack.title: Illusion Awareness - See the Frames
growTrack.learning_objective: Become aware of the motion illusion
growTrack.activity: Pause a video and advance frame by frame if you can. Notice that each frame is completely still—the motion you saw exists only in your brain's interpretation. What other 'obvious' perceptions might be constructions rather than reality?
